intro.t: Moses' last sermons, on the edge of the land.
b: A covenant document in the form of farewell speeches. Moses restates the law for a new generation who did not see Egypt, and the tone throughout is urgent: remember, do not forget, teach your children. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy more than any other book.
The heart of it is chapter 6 — love the LORD your God with all your heart, soul and strength — which Jesus identifies as the greatest commandment.

6.t: Israel's core confession: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. Jesus names the command that follows as the greatest.
The answer commanded is a story: we were slaves in Egypt and the LORD brought us out. Catechism by narrative.

8.t: The danger addressed is not famine but prosperity — that when you are full you will forget who fed you.

8.h: Man does not live on bread alone
8.t: Quoted by Jesus in the wilderness. The forty years are described as humbling and testing to reveal what was in their hearts.

18.h: Do not learn their detestable ways
18.t: Divination, mediums, consulting the dead. The alternative offered is a prophet, in the next verse.
The promise Peter applies to Jesus in Acts 3, and in the same passage the test for a false prophet: if what he says does not happen, the LORD did not speak it.

30.h: The LORD will circumcise your hearts
30.t: So that you may love him. Deuteronomy itself admits the law cannot produce what it requires.
The covenant set out as a decision with consequences. Paul picks up verses 12 to 14 in Romans 10.

34.t: He sees the land and does not enter. The book ends saying no prophet like him has since arisen — which is what makes 18:15 a promise still open.

10.t: Fear him, walk in his ways, love him, serve him. Then, startlingly, that he loves the foreigner and so should they.

29.t: Belong to the LORD; the things revealed belong to us and our children. A short verse that settles a great deal of speculation.

4.t: So that you do not forget, and so that you teach your children. Almost every exhortation in Deuteronomy runs on memory.

7.h: Why did God command the destruction of the Canaanites
7.t: This is the most serious moral objection raised against the Old Testament, and the honest starting point is what the texts actually say: the commands include women and children (Deuteronomy 20:16–18, 1 Samuel 15:3), and no Christian should pretend otherwise. Several things are true alongside that. The judgement falls on specific nations for specific practices, including child sacrifice, and Genesis 15:16 says it was delayed four hundred years until their sin reached its full measure. It is limited to one time and place and never given as a pattern for anyone since. God applied the same standard to Israel, sending them into exile for the same sins, and Rahab and her family were spared when she turned to him. Many scholars also argue that ancient war reports used deliberately sweeping language — 'left no survivors' — since the same peoples reappear shortly afterwards in the same books; others find that argument insufficient, and it does not by itself remove the commands. Christians have responded by seeing this as God's unique judicial act as judge of all the earth, by reading the conquest as a limited episode within a larger story, or by admitting they cannot fully reconcile it and holding it alongside the character of God shown at the cross. That last answer is more honest than a tidy one. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.
God's choice is traced to his love and his oath rather than to anything in them. Election stated plainly in the Old Testament.

9.t: Said three times in three verses, as if Moses expected them to miss it.

11.t: On your hands, on your foreheads, on your doorframes, talked about at home and on the road. Faith passed on by repetition rather than by event.

31.t: Said to the nation, then to Joshua, and picked up in Hebrews 13 and applied to the reader.

32.t: A national anthem of warning, to be memorised so that it testifies against them later. Verse 4 — the Rock, all his ways are just — is the best known line.

17.t: He must not accumulate horses, wives or silver, and must write out a copy of the law for himself. Solomon breaks all four.

28.t: Fourteen verses of blessing and fifty-four of curse. The imbalance is deliberate and the detail is harrowing.

1.t: It takes eleven days from Horeb to the border. It took them forty years. The book opens with that arithmetic.

2.t: Israel is told not to provoke Edom, Moab or Ammon, because God has given them their land too. God's care is not confined to Israel.

3.t: He asks and is told: enough, do not speak to me again about this. Unanswered prayer from the greatest prophet of the Old Testament.

5.t: The Sabbath reason changes from creation (Exodus 20) to rescue from Egypt. Rest is grounded in grace as well as in creation.

12.t: One sanctuary rather than many shrines. Worship is to be on God's terms, not wherever is convenient.

13.h: A prophet whose sign comes true
13.t: If he leads you after other gods, do not listen. Accurate predictions do not validate a teacher; faithfulness to God does.

14.t: Eaten in joy before the LORD, and every third year given to the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow.

15.t: Every seventh year. Verse 11 — there will always be poor people — is followed by the command to be openhanded toward them, not by resignation.

16.t: Appoint judges who will not pervert justice or take bribes. The Hebrew repeats the word for emphasis.

19.t: A system distinguishing accidental killing from murder, and protecting the innocent from revenge.

20.t: Including exemptions for the newly married, the fearful, and those who have just planted a vineyard. And do not cut down fruit trees during a siege.

21.h: Cursed is anyone hung on a tree
21.t: Paul quotes it in Galatians 3: Christ became a curse for us.

22.t: You may not ignore a stray animal. Care for a neighbour's property is written into law.

23.h: Do not return a runaway slave
23.t: A remarkable law among ancient codes, which generally required the opposite.

24.t: The text Jesus says was given because of hardness of heart. It limited abuse rather than endorsing divorce. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

25.t: Paul applies it twice to paying those who teach.

26.t: A wandering Aramean was my father — the worshipper recites the whole story when bringing the harvest.

27.t: Twelve curses, with the people answering Amen to each. Covenant accepted publicly.

33.h: The eternal God is your refuge
33.t: And underneath are the everlasting arms. Moses' final blessing.
